summary: Specifies how IRC servers manage channels, including their characteristics and properties. It covers the rules that govern how groups of users meet in a named conversation space. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: In a chat network a channel is like a clubroom. This explains the rules for who can come in, who runs the room, and how the room is kept in order.

what is channel delay in irc
subtitle: How IRC servers create, name, protect and police chat channels, from '#' rooms to collision-resistant '!' channels.

tldr.problem: IRC lets users gather in named forums called channels, but over the years several kinds of channel appeared and servers needed shared rules for how each one lives, who controls it, and what happens when the network splits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four channel name prefixes (&, #, +, !), the privileged roles of channel operator and channel creator, a set of single-letter channel modes, and mechanisms such as Channel Delay and 'safe channels' to cut down name collisions after network splits.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459 and is aimed at server implementers. It also candidly lists open problems such as mode propagation delays and weak access control.

today: RFC 2811 is an Informational memo published in April 2000. It updates RFC 1459, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is companion to the client and server protocols in RFC 2812 and RFC 2813.

sections.title: Why Channels Need Rules
sections.content:
One of the most notable features of Internet Relay Chat is that users can be grouped in forums called channels. A channel is a named group of one or more users who all receive messages addressed to that channel. It is characterized by its name, its properties and its current members.

There was originally a single type of channel. With the years new types appeared, either in response to a need or for experiments. This document specifies how servers manage channels, their characteristics and their properties.

It is mostly useful to people implementing an IRC server. Simple clients can be written without reading it, although users may find sections on channel characteristics and channel modes of interest. The document updates RFC 1459 and builds on the IRC architecture described in RFC 2810.
sections.eli5: A channel is a chat room with a name. Because there are now many kinds of rooms, the servers that run them need one shared rulebook.

sections.title: Channel Names and Scope
sections.content:
Channel names are strings of up to fifty (50) characters that begin with one of four prefix characters: ampersand, hash, plus or exclamation mark (&, #chan, +chan, !chan). Names are case insensitive. A name must not contain a space, a control G (ASCII 7) or a comma. A colon is used as the delimiter for a channel mask. Each prefix creates a distinct namespace, so there are four of them.

A channel is known to one or more servers, and a user can only join a channel known to the server they are directly connected to. The servers that know a channel must form a contiguous part of the network, so that messages can reach every member. Channels starting with & are local to the server where they are created. Other channels are known to all servers unless the name carries a channel mask, in which case only servers matching the mask (and having a local user on the channel, or neighbouring one that does) know it.

Channels starting with + do not support channel modes: every mode is unset except t, which is set.
sections.eli5: The first symbol of a room's name tells you what kind of room it is. Some rooms exist only in one building, and others are known across the whole town.

sections.title: Members, Operators and Channel Lifetime
sections.content:
To let members keep some control, a few are privileged. Only privileged members may use INVITE on an invite-only channel, KICK, MODE to change channel modes and privileges, and TOPIC on a channel where the topic is restricted. They also decide who can send in moderated channels.

Channel operators ('chanops') are shown with an @ next to their nickname in replies to NAMES, WHO and WHOIS, and ownership of the channel is shared among them. On a ! channel the user who creates it becomes the channel creator and also gets operator status. The creator can toggle certain modes that ordinary operators cannot.

Standard channels (prefixes ampersand, hash and plus) are created implicitly when the first user joins and cease to exist when the last user leaves. The creator becomes operator, except on + channels.

To avoid duplicate channels when the network splits in two, servers SHOULD NOT let a local user reuse a name if a channel operator recently left because of a split. This is known as Channel Delay. How long it lasts is tuned per network, and it does not stop a remote user from recreating the channel, which typically happens when the network rejoins.
sections.eli5: Some kids in the clubroom are helpers who can invite or remove people and change the rules. When the building splits in two, the name of a room is held for a while so nobody can sneak in and make a copy.

sections.title: Safe Channels
sections.content:
A safe channel has the prefix ! and is not created implicitly. The user sends a special JOIN in which the not-yet-known channel identifier is replaced by !. The user picks only the short name. The server prepends a channel identifier of five (5) characters, so the full name is unique and the channel is protected from abuse based on network splits.

The identifier is a function of time: the Unix time in seconds is converted to five characters using the base ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ1234567890. It therefore repeats every 36^5 seconds, about 700 days. Servers MUST also keep a list of names whose identifier is about to be used, so an attacker cannot wait for the cycle to come around.

A server MUST NOT allow a new safe channel when another channel with the same short name exists, or existed recently and lost a member to a network split. Safe channels never become unavailable and may continue to exist after the last user leaves.

If a safe channel has the r flag set and loses all its operators for longer than the reop delay, servers give operator status randomly to members. For channels of five users or fewer the rule is to reop all members once the conditions are met. For larger channels, at most one member is reopped.

The RFC admits that safe channel names are not user friendly, but says it is fairly trivial for a client program to improve on this.
sections.eli5: For a safe room, the server writes a unique code in front of the name you chose, like a ticket number. That makes it very hard for someone to make a fake copy of your room.

sections.title: Channel Modes
sections.content:
Channel properties are controlled by single-letter modes, changed with the MODE command defined in the client protocol, RFC 2812. They fall into three groups.

  • Member status: O (channel creator, set by servers only), o (operator) and v (voice, which lets a member talk on a moderated channel).
  • Flags: a anonymous, i invite-only, m moderated, n no messages from outside, q quiet (servers only), p private, s secret, r server reop, t topic restricted to operators, plus l user limit and k channel key.
  • Access masks: b ban, e exception to a ban, and I automatic invitation.

When a user asks to join, the local server checks the user's address against the ban masks. A match denies entry unless an exception mask also matches. A banned user carrying an invitation from an operator may still join. On an invite-only channel, an address that matches an invitation mask may join without being invited. Private and secret channels hide the channel from queries such as WHOIS, and the flags p and s MUST NOT both be set. Servers MAY cap the number of access masks per channel.
sections.eli5: Each channel has a panel of switches. One switch makes it invitation only, one makes only some people able to talk, and a list says who is banned or always welcome.

sections.title: Known Problems and Security
sections.content:
The RFC has an honest section on current problems. Because every server on a path must check a mode change, a MODE message can reach only part of the network, leaving servers disagreeing about a channel's state. When two servers connect, channel collisions are treated as inclusive events: the channel ends up with the members from both sides. If the l or k modes are set on both sides there is no rule for which value wins, and users have to fix it.

That inclusive merge is also a security weakness. It has long been used to take over channels by illegitimately gaining operator status, and it can reveal the member list or let someone receive some channel messages. The mask-based modes can be abused to waste memory and bandwidth, so a limit on their number is RECOMMENDED.

Access masks based on username and hostname are only safe if servers can authenticate connections accurately, and most public networks cannot. A channel key is sent in plaintext, so it is exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks. The anonymous flag only masks the sender as anonymous!anonymous@anonymous. between server and client, gives no anonymity between servers, and clients SHOULD show strong warnings about it.
sections.eli5: When two split chat towns reconnect, their rooms get merged, and sneaky people can use that to barge in. Passwords are sent where others could read them, so the rooms are not perfectly secret.

items.label: Channel creator
items.desc: Gives channel creator status; only used on safe channels, set by servers.

items.label: Operator
items.desc: Give or take channel operator privilege.

items.label: Voice
items.desc: Give or take the right to talk on a moderated channel.

items.label: Invite only
items.desc: New members need an invitation or a matching invite mask.

items.label: Moderated
items.desc: Only operators and voiced members may send.

items.label: Quiet
items.desc: For servers only; joins, parts and nick changes are not shown.

items.label: Private
items.desc: Conceals the channel from other users.

items.label: Secret
items.desc: Conceals the channel even more than private.

items.label: Server reop
items.desc: Servers re-assign operators when none remain.

items.label: Topic lock
items.desc: Only operators can change the topic.

items.label: Key
items.desc: Set or remove the channel key (password).

items.label: User limit
items.desc: Set or remove the limit on members.
